S1: In October, India's central bank raised interest rates for the first time in more than three years. And in America, markets now expect the Federal Reserve to raise rates in December. After years of cuts, rates are going up again. So what does that actually mean for your loan, your rent, and your savings? Let's walk through it, in about four minutes.
S2: Think of a central bank as the bank for banks. When your bank needs money overnight, it borrows at the central bank's rate. In India, that's the repo rate, now five point five percent. In the United States, it's the federal funds rate, now between three point seven five and four percent. When that rate goes up, money becomes more expensive for every bank in the country.
S3: So why would anyone make money more expensive on purpose? One word: inflation. When prices rise too fast, a central bank raises rates, so people borrow and spend a little less, and prices cool down. This year, oil jumped above one hundred dollars a barrel during the conflict in West Asia, and that pushed up the cost of almost everything that has to be made or moved. Central banks are trying to stop that from becoming permanent.
S4: Here's the chain. The central bank raises its rate. Banks now pay more to borrow, so they charge more to lend. Floating-rate home loans, car loans and business loans reset higher. And companies paying more interest often pass some of it on in their prices, and in rents. It doesn't happen overnight, but within a few months, it shows up in your monthly payments.
S5: Let's put a number on it. Take a four hundred thousand dollar home loan, over thirty years. At six point two five percent, the payment is about two thousand, four hundred and sixty-three dollars a month. At six point five percent, it's about two thousand, five hundred and twenty-eight. Just a quarter of a percent adds sixty-five dollars, every single month. That's about twenty-three thousand, five hundred dollars over the life of the loan.
S6: Now, many banks don't raise your payment at all. Instead, they quietly make your loan longer. Your E M I stays the same, but you pay for more months, and that usually costs far more. On a fifty lakh rupee loan over twenty years, a quarter-point rise means paying about seven hundred and eighty rupees more each month, around one point nine lakh extra in total. Keep the same E M I instead, and the loan runs about a year longer, costing nearly five lakh. So if your bank extends your loan, ask about raising the E M I instead.
S7: There is good news too. When rates rise, banks usually pay more on fixed deposits and savings. If you have cash sitting idle, it's worth comparing deposit rates now. Just remember, a higher rate only really helps if it beats inflation.
S8: So, rising rates mean dearer loans, a little relief for savers, and a good reason to check your own numbers. You can do that free at calc souq dot com.
